Why Voter ID
Our democracy relies on confidence in our elections, but Californians’ trust is fading. Voters are concerned about election security thanks, in part, to issues like unchecked ballot harvesting, lack of citizenship verification, and inconsistent signature reviews. A bombshell report by the non-partisan Transparency Foundation gives California a failing grade on election practices.
"From its failure to maintain accurate voter registration lists to its refusal to verify the identity and eligibility of voters, California by far has the worst election practices in the nation."
-Transparency California
We are launching a transformative campaign, bringing a common-sense constitutional amendment to the 2026 ballot to restore order, fairness, and trust in California’s elections.
The Voter ID Initiative: A Two-Step Solution
The proposed amendment, Proposition 39 , will:
Require Voter ID for Every Ballot Counted: All votes, whether cast in-person or by mail, will be counted only after verification of a government-issued identification.
Citizenship Verification: Require the Secretary of State and county elections officials to use government data to verify citizenship attestations on voter registrations, closing loopholes and protecting voter rolls from error or abuse.
These basic safeguards will not hinder legal voting, but guarantee each valid vote is protected.
Widespread Support for Voter ID
This is not a partisan issue; it’s a matter of validity and common sense. Poll after poll shows that Californians overwhelmingly support Voter ID requirements:
In January 2026, a Public Opinion Strategies poll showed 79% support for citizenship verification and 68% for voter ID, including 93% of Republicans, 70% of Independents, and 52% of Democrats.
In late April 2025, UC Berkeley IGS Poll found that 71% of registered voters support a proof of citizenship requirement to vote, including 95% of Republicans, 59% of Democrats, and 71% of voters registered with other parties or as “no-party-preference.”
As of March 2026, this Voter ID Initiative has officially turned in more than 1.3 million signatures in all 58 counties in California. With overwhelming support from across the state and data from multiple polls, it’s clear that Voter ID is a unifying, popular solution whose time has come.
Why It Matters – Now
Recent expansions of mail-in voting, automatic registration, and suspension of safeguards have put trust in elections at risk. States with Voter ID laws and citizenship checks tend to enjoy higher public confidence and fewer election disputes. It’s time for California to adopt a system we can trust.
Voter ID does not eliminate mail-in ballots; it updates a system to ensure that each ballot is counted accurately. It gives all California voters an extra layer of trust in the election process.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

PROP
02
CALIFORNIA Strengthens State Rainy Day Fund
Purpose
Proposition 2 is a constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the legislature, that would
strengthen California’s rainy day fund by increasing the cap on how much money the state can set
aside each year. The measure also would make it easier for the state to use tax revenues to pay
down debt.1
Research Assistant: Arushi Goyal ’28
Background
The Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), also known as the rainy day fund,
is California’s largest state budget reserve. The state uses this fund to save
money when revenues are strong and to reduce cuts to public services when
revenues are weak. This fund is especially important in California because
the state’s revenues depend heavily on taxes on the incomes of high-income
residents, which can vary greatly from year to year, thus creating “boom and
bust” budget cycles.2
The state automatically sets aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues each year.
It also sets aside “excess” capital gains revenues in years when they exceed
8% of General Fund tax revenues. Generally, the state deposits 50% of these
set-aside revenues into the rainy day fund and uses the other 50% to pay
down certain types of state debt. Currently, the state can use these excess
revenues to pay down only pension and retiree health debt, and cannot make
extra payments on other forms of debt such as unemployment insurance
debt and certain education and Medi-Cal obligations. This requirement is
set to end in 2030, after which some or all of that money may be put into the
rainy day fund.3
Under current law, the rainy day fund is capped at 10% of estimated General
Fund tax revenues. When this limit is reached, any dollars that would other-
wise go into the rainy day fund must be spent on infrastructure.4 California
also has a constitutional spending cap, commonly known as the Gann Limit,
which was passed by the voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year for infation and population
growth.5 Most spending counts toward this limit, including money deposited
into reserves. Withdrawals from state reserves during budget emergencies
do not count against the Gann Limit, but when state revenues are high, the
spending cap can limit California’s ability to build its reserves.
The rainy day fund can be tapped only during a budget emergency. The gover-
nor must formally declare an emergency before deposits can be reduced or
suspended or money can be withdrawn. The declaration can come late in the
fscal year, sometimes after the legislature’s deadline to pass a budget. This
can leave lawmakers passing a budget that assumes an emergency before
one is ofcially declared.6
In the state legislature the vote to place this measure on the ballot was 59-8
in the Assembly and 29-2 in the Senate.7
Proposal
If approved, Proposition 2 would:8
• Double the BSA cap from 10% to 20% of
estimated General Fund tax revenues.
• Set aside more General Fund revenues during
“boom” years.
• Expand the types of state debt that may be paid
down with set-aside revenues.
• Extend the debt-paydown requirement by 10
years, to 2039-40.
• Change how rainy day fund and other deposits
count toward the Gann Limit.
• Create a simpler process for declaring a budget
emergency.
Fiscal Impact
The LAO estimates that Proposition 2 would
increase the state’s budget reserves. Having more
money in the BSA would make it easier for the
state to balance its budget during downturns. The
measure could also cause the state to pay down
debt more aggressively.9

CALIFORNIA Makes permanent existing voter-approved income tax rates for high-income
Californians
Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave of cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5

ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Proposal
Proposition 3, ofcially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for infation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county ofces of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected ofcials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10
Fiscal Impact
If the current income tax rates are allowed
to expire as scheduled, the California
Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) estimates
that the state would lose between $5 billion
and $15 billion in annual revenue beginning
in 2031.11 For context, this year the state
plans to spend about $250 billion from
the General Fund, with about half of that
spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12

Prop
39
CA
Prop
39
|
Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification
Requires voters to present a government-issued identification card at the polls or the last four digits of a government-issued identification number when voting by mail.
SPUR's Recommendation
California already has safeguards to protect election integrity. When registering, voters certify eligibility under penalty of perjury and provide identifying information. In-person voters state their name and address and sign the roster, while signature verification is used for vote-by-mail ballots. Illegal voting is a felony. California has no evidence of widespread voter fraud, despite allegations following the 2020 presidential election. Research has found that strict voter ID requirements can create barriers for voters who lack acceptable identification.
In September 2024, California enacted SB 1174, which prohibits local governments — including charter cities — from requiring voters to present identification to vote unless required by state or federal law. Prop. 39 would override this prohibition and establish a statewide voter ID requirement.
Implementing the strict voter ID requirements in this proposition could impose high costs on state and local governments. Without evidence of widespread voter fraud, adding barriers to voting and imposing significant implementation costs on already-strained public budgets is not a good investment.
Vote NO
What Prop. 39 Would Do
Proposition 39 would amend the California Constitution to add three new requirements to statewide voter rules:
Voters would need to present government-issued identification to vote in person or provide the last four digits of a government-issued identification number to vote by mail.
The state would be required to provide a free voter identification card to any voter who requests one.
The Secretary of State and county elections officials would be required to verify voters’ citizenship attestations and annually report the percentage of each county’s voter rolls that have been citizenship-verified.
The proposition language does not specify which forms of ID would qualify or how citizenship would be verified. Instead, it authorizes the Legislature to pass implementing legislation to work out those details after voters pass the initiative.
The Backstory
The federal Voting Rights Act of 1965 (VRA) was enacted to protect the constitutional right to vote for Black Americans and other minority groups. For decades, it provided federal oversight of elections in jurisdictions with histories of discrimination. However, recent Supreme Court decisions have weakened key VRA provisions. As a result, states face fewer barriers to adopting stricter voter ID laws, reducing early voting, closing polling locations, and changing election procedures, raising concerns about voter access and representation.
Under the 2002 Help America Vote Act, all first-time voters in federal elections who registered by mail must show ID. California also verifies voter identity with a driver’s license number, state identification number, or the last four digits of a Social Security number when registering people to vote, attesting under penalty of perjury that they are U.S. citizens. In addition, states verify signatures on vote-by-mail ballots.
Since the 2020 presidential election, public claims of voter fraud have increased, despite extremely low instances in U.S. elections. 1 Currently, 36 states require some form of identification at polling sites. Of those, only nine states have “strict” voter ID laws that require a voter to present an ID (some states require a photo ID; others do not) to cast a ballot. Voters without proper ID must cast a provisional ballot and then take additional steps before their ballot is officially counted. In the remaining 27 “non-strict” voter ID states, voters without proper ID can sign an affidavit verifying their identity (subject to perjury). 2
State Voter ID Requirements as of 2020
Source: National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
Recently, Republican Party leaders have made efforts to enact voter ID laws in California. In September 2024, the state Legislature passed Senate Bill 1174, which prohibits local governments in California from enacting their own voter ID requirements. The state then sued Huntington Beach over its 2024 voter ID measure, arguing that state election law preempted it. In January 2026, the California Supreme Court sided with the state and struck down Huntington Beach’s local voter ID requirement.
In January 2025, Assemblymember Carl DeMaio introduced the California Voter ID and Election Integrity Act of 2025 (Assembly Bill 25), pursuing a legislative path to a statewide voter ID law. The bill failed on a party-line vote in April 2025. This year, a federal voter ID law, H.R.7296, the SAVE America Act, was introduced to Congress. If H.R. 7296 were to pass, voters in all states would be required to present photo identification showing U.S. citizenship when voting, preempting state laws.
Assemblymember DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, pursued the voter initiative process this year and gathered signatures for Prop. 39. If passed, California would join the nine states with strict voter ID requirements. Prop. 39 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Research consistently finds that voters of color, low-income individuals, elderly voters, students, people with disabilities, and those who recently changed their names are less likely to possess the specific government-issued IDs required under strict voter ID laws and are more likely to face barriers to obtaining them. 3 Costs — including fees for birth certificates and other documents, transportation to government offices, and time away from work — can create additional burdens. 4 Researchers have documented racial disparities in ID possession and evidence that strict voter ID requirements can widen racial turnout gaps. Approximately 13% of Black Americans lack acceptable voter ID, compared with 5% of white Americans, making voter ID laws a significant equity issue. 5
Pros
SPUR could not identify any benefits to this measure.
Cons
Studies have found that voter ID laws do not reduce actual or perceived voter fraud. 6
Government-issued ID requirements can create barriers for eligible voters, increase ballot rejections from data-entry errors, slow voting, and disproportionately affect people who face challenges taking time off work, traveling to obtain ID, or securing required documentation.
Including partial ID numbers with names and addresses on mail-ballot envelopes (as would be required under this proposition) could increase privacy and identity-theft risks when combined with information exposed through other data breaches. 7
Prop. 39 would impose additional costs on state and local governments, with estimated one-time costs in the tens of millions of dollars and ongoing annual costs ranging from tens to hundreds of millions, depending on future legislative requirements. 8

Issue Brief
Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.
Table Of Contents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Is Part of a Nationwide Effort to Restrict Voting and Limit People’s Say in Policymaking
California Should Continue to Promote Voter Participation and Improve the Election Process
Prop. 39 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law
Californians are required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/who-can-vote-california) to be US citizens to vote. 1 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2101.). There are two exceptions: Oakland and San Francisco allow certain noncitizens to vote in local school board elections. To register to vote, a person must declare in writing, under penalty of perjury, that they meet all voter eligibility requirements, including that they are a US citizen (https://covr.sos.ca.gov/). 2 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2150.). Under federal law (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra), state motor vehicle agencies — like California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) — must provide residents with the opportunity to register to vote when they apply for or renew a driver’s license or state ID card and/or change their address. In California, this is known as Motor Voter (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions). DMV customers who indicate that they are eligible to vote are registered to vote by the Secretary of State (SOS) unless they opt out. However, the DMV does not send to the SOS (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions) information regarding customers who indicate they are not eligible to vote. Falsely claiming to be a US citizen on a voter registration application and attempting to vote would expose a person to state felony charges as well as the possibility of deportation under federal law. 3 (javascript:void(0)) For example, see California Elections Code, Section 18560(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.), 8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(6)(a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1227&num=0&edition=prelim), and 18 U.S.C. Section 611 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/611).
In addition, state law makes it a crime to:
Vote or attempt to vote more than once in an election,
Impersonate or attempt to impersonate a voter in an election, or
Apply for or cast a vote-by-mail ballot by fraudulently signing the name of a fake person, another qualified voter, or a person who is not qualified to vote. 4 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 18560(b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.) and Section 18578 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18578.).
A person who is convicted of any of these crimes could be imprisoned for up to three years.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require state and county election officials to “use best efforts” to verify, using “government data,” that registered voters are US citizens. The measure does not define “best efforts” or what constitutes “government data.” In addition, election officials would have to annually report the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Present Additional Identifying Information When They Cast Their Ballot
Current Law
All states, including California, already have voter ID requirements (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification) as required by federal law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards). For example, to register to vote, Californians must provide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) a California driver’s license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security Number (SSN) if they lack a driver’s license or ID card. Californians who lack a driver’s license, a state ID card, or a SSN are assigned a unique identifier (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to validate their registration. Californians generally are not required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to present an ID when voting. 5 (javascript:void(0)) Californians may need to show (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) an acceptable form of ID when they vote by mail or in person if all of the following apply: 1) they’re voting for the first time in a federal election, 2) they registered by mail or online, and 3) they did not provide a California ID or SSN when registering. Acceptable forms of ID (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) include, but aren’t limited to, a California driver’s license or state ID card, a US passport, a student or military ID, a utility bill, and a bank statement.
When voting by mail, California voters sign the outside of their ballot envelope, and elections officials verify the signature before counting the ballot. 6 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 3011(a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3011.) and Section 3019 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.). Voters must be given an opportunity to correct or “cure” their ballot if they failed to sign the envelope or if their signature does not match the signature on file. 7 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Sections 3019(c)-(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.).
When voting in person, California voters state their name and address and sign a list of registered voters under penalty of perjury. 8 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 14216(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216.). While election officials do not verify (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) the signatures of in-person voters before counting their ballots, counties have procedures in place to prevent voter fraud. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For example, in many counties, poll workers are able to look up voting records in real time to ensure that a voter has not already cast a ballot in the election. This applies to counties that participate (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act/vca-participating-counties) in California’s Voter’s Choice Act (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) as well as to counties that have adopted the Sign, Scan, and Go (https://www.placercountyelections.gov/sign-scan-go/) option. As noted above, it is a crime in California to fraudulently vote in an election, to vote more than once, or to impersonate another voter. Penalties range from up to one year in a county jail to up to three years in state prison.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would impose new requirements on Californians to cast a ballot in person or mail a ballot.
To vote in person:
Voters would have to present a “government-issued” ID when they arrive at their polling place. Prop. 39 does not specifically define what “government-issued” ID means, so the Legislature would need to clarify which types of ID a voter could present to prove their identity. 10 (javascript:void(0)) Prop. 39 says broadly that “government-issued” ID “means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity.”
To vote by mail:
All new and existing voters would have to select a “government-issued” ID that would be reflected in their “voter registration record.” This requirement effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register to provide their chosen ID to election officials.
When voting, voters would have to write on the outside of their ballot envelope the last four digits of a “unique identifying number” from the “government-issued” ID that they selected for the purpose of voting. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The government-issued ID that voters choose for this purpose would have to subsequently be made available to them “on request by phone or electronically.”
Election officials would verify that the four digits written on the envelope match the last four digits of the ID number in the voter’s registration record.
Requires the State to Create a New Voter ID Card
Current Law
California currently allows Californians to apply for three types of ID cards (https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/driver-licenses-identification-cards/identification-id-cards/) in addition to drivers’ licenses that are used to prove identity or age. 12 (javascript:void(0)) The ID cards are issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as alternatives to a driver’s license and cannot be used to operate a motor vehicle.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the state to provide a voter ID card to eligible voters who request one. Voters could use this optional ID as their “government-issued” ID for voting by mail or in person. This card would be provided to voters free of charge.
Requires Ongoing State Audits of How the State and Counties Are Complying with Prop. 39
Current Law
California’s independently elected (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-state-constitutional-offices-defined/) Secretary of State oversees (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/about-agency) all elections in the state, including ensuring election laws are enforced, testing and approving voting equipment, compiling election returns, and certifying election results.
In addition, California’s independent, nonpartisan State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/) conducts performance audits and investigations of various state and local government agencies and recommends solutions for improving services. However, the State Auditor currently does not have a formal, ongoing role in auditing California’s elections or evaluating election administration.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the State Auditor, in odd-numbered years, to audit state and county compliance with Prop. 39 and report any recommendations for improvement.
Requires the State Legislature to Pass Laws to Implement Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the Legislature to “promptly enact laws” to implement the measure. For example, legislators would have to define which kinds of “government-issued” ID would be acceptable for voting as well as clarify what it means to make a “best effort” to verify a voter’s citizenship status. Prop. 39 would also require the Legislature to establish rules for military and overseas voters that are consistent with federal law.
Allows Citizens to Sue the State or Any County for Not Complying with Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would allow private citizens to sue the state and/or any county for any alleged noncompliance with the initiative. The measure does not specify what kind of evidence would be required to file a lawsuit.
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Would Waste Resources By Addressing a Nonexistent Problem
The voter ID requirements that Prop. 39 would establish provide a “solution” to a nonexistent problem. This measure is based on the false premise that voter fraud — casting a ballot when one is not eligible to vote — is undermining election integrity. However, research shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare. For example:
Using a comprehensive database tracking election fraud (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-widespread-is-election-fraud-in-the-united-states-not-very/) that was created by the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, the Brookings Institute found across more than 200 federal elections held in recent decades, the share of fraudulent votes cast were infinitesimally small — ranging from roughly 3 to 15 votes out of 10 million in seven states with close election outcomes. The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”
Additionally, while proponents of Prop. 39 argue that imposing additional ID requirements will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, evidence for this claim is lacking. One study (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf) found that registered voters had roughly equal confidence that votes were counted accurately whether they were in states with strict voter ID laws or states with the minimum ID requirements mandated by federal law.
Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of California Riverside and Western Washington University looking at voter perceptions in 2014 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1532440015624102?) and following the 2020 US presidential election (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129231206179) found that strict voter ID laws and the quality of election administration more generally had little to no effect on voter confidence. This and other research (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129241283169) suggests this may be because voters view election laws through a partisan lens and their confidence may be more heavily influenced by partisan rhetoric and whether their preferred candidate wins or loses an election. 13 (javascript:void(0)) See Lonna Rae Atkeson, Eli McKown-Dawson, and Robert M. in California Today?

and Knowledge

BACKGROUND
Coming out of the contentious 2000 general elections both the states and US federal
government ushered in a wide range of changes to our electoral system. What identification, if
any, is necessary to register and/or vote has become one of the longest standing and
contentious debates. Georgia was one of the first states in the country to adopt a strict photo ID
requirement for those seeking to vote in-person.1 Since that time the states have adopted a
wide range of laws that request or require a photo ID. Additionally, the federal government and a
growing number of states have pursued policies that would add additional requirements to show
documentary proof of citizenship during the voter registration process.
In light of policy discussions regarding voter ID and proof-of-citizenship legislation in California
and nationally, VoteRiders and the Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement (CDCE) at the
University of Maryland contracted with SSRS, a highly regarded survey firm, to survey a
representative sample of the California adult US citizen population. Our primary goal was to
examine the extent to which adult citizens in California have the ID they might need in order to
vote if California changes its voter ID law. Since documents are not currently needed for most
California voters when voting,2 this allows us to provide a sensitivity analysis that explores how
various provisions could impact the number of people who would be able to vote with the ID
they have. We also sought to gauge Californian’s understanding of current voter ID laws, and to
assess attitudes about the expense and wait time to get key documents to prove identity and
citizenship in California. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first survey of voting eligible
Californians with questions specifically about the types of identification voting eligible
Californians have.3 This research builds on national survey research conducted in 2023 and
state surveys in Georgia and Texas.4
The sample of 1,561 respondents was drawn from SSRS’s probability panel with a supplement
from the Verasight probability panel. Included in the sample are oversamples of
18-24-year-olds, Black respondents, and naturalized citizens. The survey was fielded November
19, 2025 - December 8, 2025. All of the results below are weighted. The survey instrument was

A NEW FRAMEWORK FOR THINKING ABOUT ID LAWS
A look across the country reveals that there are a wide variety of voter identification laws in
place. For states that elect to request or require that potential voters provide documentary ID
when voting, we find it most useful to characterize the laws based on how comprehensive and
flexible they are. By comprehensive we mean how many options there are for potential voters
to meet their state’s main expectations during the voting process with respect to the forms of ID
that are accepted. States choose how comprehensive the law is along the following dimensions:
● Form of ID (e.g. driver’s license, state ID card, gun permit, public college ID, utility bill)
● Photo or not
● Degree of name match
● Address match
● Government issuing the ID, including out-of-state
● Expiration date
By flexible we mean what options are available to those who do not meet the main
requirements when they are attempting to vote. Here, the primary options, some of which are
used together, include:
● Provisional ballot, and whether follow up by the voter to provide ID is needed
● Signature match
● Providing biographical information (e.g. birth date)
● Signing an affidavit
● Vouching (e.g. a poll worker can vouch to verify the individuals identity)
For example, if the California legislature opts to or is required to enact a new voter ID
law, it will have to decide how comprehensive and flexible to make the law. As of this
writing, except for a specific type of new voter (see footnote 2), Californians voting in person
state their name and address and sign the poll book. Election officials verify they are registered
voters through a review of the poll book. California is a vote-by-mail state, so all registered
voters receive a ballot in the mail. Voters who choose to vote by mail must sign the return
envelope. Election officials compare the signature on the envelope with the signature on the
voter registration record.

RESULTS
We begin our analysis with an examination of driver’s licenses, exploring how variations in the
comprehensiveness of a potential voter ID law in California might influence the proportion of
Californians who have a driver’s license they could use to vote if the law changes. We then
examine state ID cards, and other forms of ID to estimate the proportion of Californians who do
not have any government issued photo ID or no government issued ID at all. The next section
provides details about how rates of ownership of key types of ID vary by demographics and
party ID. We conclude with an analysis of potential confusion around the current voter ID laws in
California and attitudes about the cost and wait time to receive documents one might need to
replace.
SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS
Driver’s Licenses
Nearly 2.7 million Californians do not have a current (non-expired) driver’s license at all.
Just under 11%, or about 2.7 million people, who are U.S. citizens aged 18 or older in California
do not have a driver’s license, from California or any other state, current or expired. The majority
of Californians (77%) have a current (non-expired) license with both their current name and
address. Under any voter ID regime that does not also include proof of citizenship, these 77%
would be able to use their CA license to vote.
The remaining group of Californians (nearly 13%) have a license, but it has an address that is
not current, a name that is not current, is expired, is from another state, or has some
combination of those features. The bulk of those in this category are those who have a current
CA license with their current name but with an old address (7%, or about 1.8 million people).
With regard to identity, those individuals would not face any issues, as the name and photo
could be used, but verification of residency would require another document. The next largest
group (3%, or about 650k people) have a current out-of-state-license with their current name.
About 2.5%, or 630k Californians, have an expired CA license. Within that group, the largest
categories are those who have an expired CA license with their current name and address
(1.4% of Californians), and those who have an expired CA license with their current name but
an old address (1% of Californians). A small percentage of Californians have a license with a
name that is not current; having a former address is much more common. See Figure 1.
Whether those who have a license but not one that is from CA, that is current (non-expired), and
has their current name and address could use their license to vote would depend on how a new
law is written. The most comprehensive approach would allow over 3 million Californians to use
their license in addition to the 77% of Californians (about 19.4 million) who have a current
(non-expired) CA license with current name and address. That is, focusing only on driver’s
licenses, allowing for an old address would allow nearly 1.8 million Californians to use
their current (non-expired) CA license, allowing an out-of-state license would allow
another 650k to use their license, and allowing an expired CA license would add another
630k to the list of those who could use their license. Allowing for other features (such as an
expired out-of-state license) would add more, but our estimates suggest these additions would
be relatively small.

Other ID
The primary tool to prove identity for those without a driver’s license is the official state ID card.
While the majority of Californians without a driver’s license have an official CA state ID
card, 24% do not. That is, overall 2.6% of Californians do not have any driver’s license or
official state ID card at all. This translates to over 650,000 Californians.
When we ask about a variety of other IDs such as passport, military ID, and student ID, we find
that 1.5% of Californians, or about 385k, do not have a non-expired license, non-expired state
ID, or other non-expired government issued photo ID. Those facing a potential problem using an
ID to vote drops to 1.1% if IDs that are expired, from another state, or from a private high school
or college are included as viable. Our estimates indicate that about 0.8% of Californians, or
just under 200k, do not have any government issued ID at all, including government ID
that does not have a photo. These results are summarized in Figure 2 below.
Several forms of ID stand out as particularly common among those who might need to use ID
other than a driver’s license or official state ID card if CA changes their ID law (see Table 1).
Among those who do not have a driver’s license or official state ID card at all 29% have a
current passport that is readily accessible, 9% have an expired passport that is readily
accessible, and 13% have a current public school ID (high school or college). Among those who
have a license or and/or official state ID card but that might not be able to use it if a new CA law
is not particularly comprehensive (with regard to expiration date, issuing state, name match, and
address match again) current passports that are readily accessible (48%) are the most common
form of ID. This is followed by a current military ID (26%), current public school ID (high school
or college) (19%), readily accessible expired passport (14%), and a current government
employee ID (13%).

DRIVER’S LICENSE OWNERSHIP BY INDIVIDUAL CHARACTERISTICS
Millions of Californians across political parties do not have a license. Eleven percent of
Democrats (1.4 million people), 4% of Republicans (350,000 people), and 21% of
independents/others (825,000 people) indicate they do not have a license at all.
Californian people of color are disproportionately less likely to have a current driver’s
license. Nineteen percent of Asian American/Pacific Islanders, 18% of Black Californians, and
14% of Hispanic Californians do not have a driver’s license, compared to just 3% of White
Californians.
Young Californians are less likely to have a driver’s license. About 8% of Californians age
25 or older do not have a license, while 35% of Californians ages 18-24 do not have a license at
all, which we estimate to be over one-million Californians.7
People with less education and lower annual incomes are more likely to lack a current
driver’s license. Twenty-seven percent of people without a high school degree do not have a
driver’s license at all. Twenty-two percent of high school graduates and 11% of those with some
post-high school education do not have a license compared to 4% of college graduates and 1%
of those with some post-college education. Californians with annual incomes under $30,000 are
disproportionately less likely to have a license, with 34% not having a license at all. By
comparison, 7% of those making between $30,000 and $50,000 annually, 6% making between
$50,000 and $100,000 and 2% of those making over $100,000 do not have a license at all.
People with a disability are far more likely to lack a current driver’s license. Twenty-two
percent of people who self-identified as having a disability do not have a license at all,
compared to 8% of non-disabled people.
Californians provided a variety of reasons to explain why they do not have a driver’s
license. The most common reasons include “Driving makes me anxious/afraid” (14%) and “I
can’t drive for medical reasons or a disability” (14%). Some people do not have a license
because they “don’t like driving/don’t drive” (11%) or they are “not interested” (6%). Twenty-six
percent of individuals without a driver’s license cite bureaucratic or economic factors as
the reasons for which they do not have a license, including the cost of getting a license
(6%), cost of buying a car (9%), cost of car insurance (3%), lack of underlying documents (3%),
or because “the process is too complicated” (5%).
Passports are another common type of photo ID. Sixty-percent of Californians have an
unexpired passport with their current name, but 24% do not have a passport at all. Two in
ten Democrats and Republicans do not have a passport (21% and 22% respectively), compared
to 37% of independents. Black Californians are disproportionately less likely to have a passport
(53%) than Hispanic Californians (26%) and White Californians (19%). The overwhelming

DOCUMENTARY PROOF OF CITIZENSHIP
Over 3 million voting-age Californians who are US citizens (14%) would have difficulty
showing documentation proving their citizenship (documentary proof of citizenship, or
DPOC). Documents proving citizenship include US Birth Certificates, US passports or passport
cards, US Naturalization Certificates, and US Certificates of Citizenship.8 525,000 Californians
(2%) do not have any DPOC at all, while 7% cannot readily access their DPOC.9 Six
percent of Californians report they can easily access their DPOC documents, but their
documents do not reflect their current legal name.
AAPI Californians are less likely to have difficulties producing documentary proof of citizenship
compared to other racial groups. 9 in 10 AAPI Californians can readily access some form of
DPOC that reflects their current name (92%), compared to 81% of Black Californians, 85% of
Hispanic Californians, and 86% of White Californians. However, AAPI Californians and Hispanic
Californians are twice as likely as Black Californians to report not having any DPOC at all (4%
and 2%, respectively), and just 1% of White Californians do not have any DPOC. Different racial
groups experience different difficulties with providing DPOC. Fifteen percent of Black
Californians have trouble accessing their DPOC, compared to 3% of AAPI Californians, 7% of
Hispanic Californians, and 6% of White Californians. Meanwhile, 9% of White Californians have
DPOC with the wrong name, compared to 1% of AAPI Californians, 2% of Black Californians,
and 5% of Hispanic Californians.
Similarly, men and women have different problems with providing DPOC. Around 380,000
Californian men (3%) do not have any DPOC, compared to about 151,000 (just over 1%)
Californian women.10 However, 11% of Californian women report not having DPOC that
reflects their current name, but less than 1% of Californian men report the same. Similarly, 8%
of Californian women cannot easily access their DPOC, compared to 6% of Californian men.

Proposition 39
Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State's website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter's identity is established through the registration process by using their driver's license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor's Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
Proposal
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make "best efforts" using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government-Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters' identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter's registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter's identify when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
Fiscal Effects
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote-for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.

Proposition 39
Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State's website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter's identity is established through the registration process by using their driver's license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor's Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
Proposal
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make "best efforts" using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government-Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters' identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter's registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter's identify when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
Fiscal Effects
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote-for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.

State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.
