TESTIMONY OF DAVID BECKER
Executive Director and Founder, The Center for Election Innovation & Research
BEFORE THE CALIFORNIA STATE SENATE
August 26, 2025
Good morning, and thank you for inviting me to testify on the important issue of verifying voters’
identities. I’m David Becker, the Executive Director and Founder of the nonpartisan, nonprofit,
Center for Election Innovation & Research, based in Washington, DC. We work with election
officials of both parties, all around the nation, to support elections that voters should and do
trust.
The issue of identity verification can often become highly politicized. But I have worked with the
professionals who run our elections for over 25 years, and almost all will tell you, regardless of
their party, that they want a system where every voter is verifiable, but also where no eligible
voter could be disenfranchised. The idea of a single fraudulent ballot, or a single
disenfranchised voter, are equally troubling to them. Election officials, law enforcement, and
academic studies all confirm that voter fraud, and in particular, voter impersonation fraud, are
extremely rare.
And as you know, California and indeed every state already has processes in place to verify the
identity of voters, from federally-required ID to register, pursuant to the Help America Vote Act of
2002, to processes to confirm the identity of voters at the polling place or confirm the identity of
those returning mail ballots.
That said, several states across the political spectrum have sought to strengthen these
provisions, and there are several examples where states have developed systems that meet the
dual goals of ensuring integrity, while preserving access for all eligible voters.
Let’s start with mail ballot verification, since that’s how the majority of Californians cast their
ballots. Several states have innovated to make mail ballot verification more accurate and more
efficient. Georgia, for instance, requires a drivers license number or state ID number on their
returned mail ballots. If the voter has neither, they can give the last four digits of their Social
Security Number. In Georgia, having neither in the voter file is extremely rare – 99.94% of all
Georgia voters have either a state ID or Social Security number in their voter file.
Minnesota similarly requires a drivers license, state ID, or Social Security number. Virginia
requires the last four digits of the Social Security Number, plus the year of birth. Importantly, if a
voter fails to include the identification numbers (which happens rarely), or if a match proves
difficult, these states all have failsafes, such as a signature match, to allow for the ballot to be
counted. These states have generally found that such methods reduce the amount of time it
takes to verify mail ballots, while maintaining or enhancing their ability to confirm identity of the
voter.
And some counties are experimenting further, with King County, Washington, piloting a “pre-
verification” process where voters can go online and submit their ID number and have their
identity verified before election officials even receive the ballot.
These innovations have been enormously popular, with large bipartisan majorities expressing
support. 91.5% of those that used King County’s new “pre-verification” said they’d use it again,
for instance.
With regard to in-person voting, the options for secure, non-disenfranchising voter ID, have
been tested over decades. The most common, and successful form of voter ID implemented in
states have been those that offer an affidavit alternative for eligible voters, in those rare cases
where they don’t have, or can’t get, the requisite ID. States as diverse as Connecticut,
Delaware, Idaho, Louisiana, Michigan, South Dakota, and Virginia require some form of ID
when a voter casts a ballot in person, but if they don’t have ID at the time they vote, the voter
can fill out an affidavit with identifying information and an oath under penalty of perjury, and cast
a regular ballot.
This enables states to ensure that no eligible voters are disenfranchised, while also preventing
those rare cases of voter impersonation fraud, and providing an evidentiary base to investigate
potential cases. The Idaho Secretary of State reported that only 0.2% of all voters in 2024 used
an affidavit, and further confirms that “there are no known instances of voters misrepresenting
themselves on an affidavit.” Michigan found an similar rate of 0.2% affidavits used in the 2020
election.
You’ll note that this group of states spans the political spectrum. It’s true that there are efforts to
implement extremely-restrictive voter ID laws in some states, which could disenfranchise some
eligible voters who lack ID. But if California decides to amend its voter identification laws, other
states have demonstrated that there are ways to do it without disenfranchising eligible voters,
and in the case of mail ballots, perhaps building efficiencies that could result in faster, more
accurate counting of ballots.
Thak you, and I’m happy to answer any questions you might have.

Literature Review Methodology
8/21/2025 18
A search for academic and advocacy research pieces on voter fraud in California since the 2020 election cycle involved
multiple search tools, including Google, Google Scholar, journal databases (such as those available on the California
State Library’s online resources webpage), university-adjacent research organizations (such as Harvard University’s
Electoral Integrity Project), all 58 counties’ Grand Jury websites, and ChatGPT.
Searches utilized key terms, such as “election fraud,” “voter fraud,” or “election integrity,” which were identified as
common terms used in research relevant to this topic. Searches were filtered such that research on elections prior to
2020 were not included. Additionally, research that was topic-adjacent, but with no specific analysis or findings related
to voter fraud (ex: a Grand Jury report talking about observations of the electoral process and commending county
staff), was excluded.

All Registered Voters Can Vote in a Primary or General Election
To register to vote in California, you must be:

18 years old or older on Election Day,

To pre-register to vote in California, you must:
Be 16 or 17 years old, and
Meet all of the other eligibility requirements to vote.
You will automatically be registered to vote on your 18th birthday.

As a voter, you will help decide who will lead us. You make your voice heard on important issues that affect the future of our state and nation. Every time you use your precious right to vote, our democracy grows stronger.
It's easy to take part in elections when you have the tools and information! Whether it's your first time voting or you are an experienced voter who has moved and just need to re-register to vote, Voting in California will give you everything you need to get started.
Here, you can apply to register to vote (http://registertovote.ca.gov/), find your polling place and learn what to expect on Election Day. You can also brush up on your rights and responsibilities as a voter, find answers to your questions about elections and voting, and get informed about the issues on the next statewide election ballot.
If you would like to vote at your local polling place select "Where and How to Vote", that page will tell you what to bring when you vote for the first time in a federal election.

Should California require voter and citizenship ID? Our Prop. 39 endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:30 PM
Ballots are dropped off at a polling location on Fountain Square Drive in Citrus Heights on Election Day, June 2, 2026. On November ballots in California, Prop. 39 seeks to require more identification from Californians before they vote.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Proposition 39 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) promises to tighten California’s elections and reduce the likelihood of voter fraud. However, the measure creates more barriers than it removes, threatening to disenfranchise legitimate voters.
Prop. 39, if passed, would change California’s voting laws by requiring voters to show government-issued identification before voting in person. For mail ballots, voters would need to provide the last four digits of a government-issued ID number, such as a driver’s license number, when submitting their ballots.
It would also require state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters are U.S. citizens. Additionally, the state would be required to issue free identification cards to voters who do not already have a qualifying ID.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 39 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html)
In practice, Prop. 39 would add a new ID requirement to safeguards California already has, resulting in more legitimate ballots being rejected than fraudulent votes being prevented.
For this reason and others, the collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/) Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urge a “no” vote on Prop. 39.
“The vast majority of registrars across the state, and that includes the Sacramento area, are doing a really good job with the tools we already have in place,” said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Law School. (https://www.lls.edu/) Levitt opposes Prop. 39, as do many prominent Democrats in California. (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316925218.html)
Federal law already requires new voters who register remotely to prove who they are through documents such as a driver’s license or passport, (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) under the Help America Vote Act, (https://www.eac.gov/about/help_america_vote_act.aspx) passed by Congress in 2002.
Julia Gomez, a staff attorney with the ACLU of Southern California who opposes Prop. 39, warns that adding another technical requirement to mail-in ballots only makes the process more difficult.
“For the June primary, county election officials rejected nearly 44,000 mail-in ballots because a voter’s signature did not match the signature on file, and more than 8,000 were rejected because the envelope lacked a signature,” Gomez noted. “That just means the voter forgot to sign the envelope. That’s 8,000 disenfranchised voters.”
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, is one of two Republican legislators behind Prop. 39. The other is state Sen. Tony Strickland, R-Huntington Beach. As The Bee reported, Prop. 39 has attracted the attention of several conservative billionaires who have invested heavily in Prop. 39.
“Backers of Proposition 39, which would also require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote, raised more than $10 million so far,” wrote The Bee’s Ben Paviour in July. “At least nine billionaires, as tracked by Forbes’ list, have invested in the fundraising committee Californians for Voter ID, which is run by Julie Luckey, the mother of tech billionaire and President Donald Trump supporter Palmer Luckey.”
Supporters of Prop. 39 tout it as a vehicle to enhance voting protections in California.
“A lot of people are sick and tired of the conspiracy theories and don’t want to have low public trust and confidence in elections, and they see voter ID as the common sense bipartisan way to fix it,” DeMaio said in Paviour’s July story. “Why is that such a mystery?”
It’s not a mystery at all. Prop. 39 is bad policy.
“A voter can accidentally leave that space blank,” Gomez said. “ They can enter the wrong number. They can transpose digits, or they can simply not understand what the instructions say.”
California doesn’t have a voter fraud crisis. It has a trust crisis, fueled by national politicians — most notably Trump—who lost elections and invented conspiracies to explain it.
We urge Californians to vote “no” on Prop. 39.

# Key findings
The closest test case is Texas. When it began requiring an ID number on mail ballots in 2022, 12.4% of mail ballots were rejected in the March primary (1 in 8), up from under 1% in 2020. By November the rate fell to 2.7% as voters adjusted. [1] [2] [3]
California already rejects about 1.7% of mail ballots (148,241 in the June 2026 primary), mostly for arriving late. Brookings found about 4 documented fraud cases per 10 million mail ballots (cases found and prosecuted, which is the only count anyone has). [2]
About 13M of 16M Californians voted by mail in 2024, so the ID-number rule would reach about 80% of voters. [4]
$17M of the Yes money came from one Illinois billionaire, Richard Uihlein. [5] [6] By Oct 26 the Yes side reported $39.5M. [7]
The sponsor, Reform California (led by Asm. Carl DeMaio), raised $5M in 2024 . [8] [6] [9] A sworn complaint pending at the FPPC alleges DeMaio used Reform California money to help his own Assembly campaign. Four earlier FPPC probes ended in two warnings and two findings of no violation. [6] [9]

# Money and conflicts
Yes $39.5M across 2 committees as of Oct 26 [7] . As of early October: Uihlein $17M, Steven Bray $3M+ in loans, Nicole Shanahan $370K, the Winklevoss twins $250K each. [5] [6]
No $33.3M across 10 committees as of Oct 26 [7] . Top donors: CA Democratic Party ~$5.5M, Graton Rancheria $2M, Patty Quillin and Quinn Delaney $1.5M each, SEIU $1M. Becerra and Speaker Rivas run a joint No committee. [5] [6]
Political scientist David McCuan says the donors may be testing a playbook for swing states like Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. [5] [6]
# Does it solve a lasting problem?
Most states require some ID at the polls [6] , and confidence in elections is a real issue. But the documented fraud it targets is rare, and the main measurable effect, based on Texas, is a temporary rise in rejected legitimate mail ballots.
# If you vote yes: accountability
Bottom line: The measure leaves the hard details to the Legislature: which databases count for checking citizenship, and what happens when a mail ballot's ID number is missing or doesn't match . [4] Those rules will decide how many legal votes get rejected. In Texas, 12.4% of mail ballots were rejected the first time a similar rule applied. [1] [2]
# Who's accountable
The Legislature must write the rules, including whether voters get a chance to fix ("cure") a missing or wrong ID number. [4]
The Secretary of State oversees statewide elections. That race (Weber vs. Wagner) is on this ballot.
County registrars verify ID numbers and citizenship. In Rancho Cucamonga, that's the San Bernardino County Registrar of Voters.
The State Auditor must report on state and county compliance every odd-numbered year. [4]
# What to ask for
A cure process for every rejected ballot, with notice by mail, text and email, and a deadline after Election Day.
County-by-county reports of rejected ballots by reason, published before and after each election.
Free ID cards that are easy to get, since the state must provide them on request. [4]
# Public records to request (CPRA)
Anyone can file a California Public Records Act request (the state's version of FOIA), with no reason required. Agencies must respond within 10 days, or 24 in unusual cases. [12]
To the San Bernardino County Registrar of Voters: Under the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code § 7920.000 et seq.), I request the number of vote-by-mail ballots challenged and rejected in the November 2024 and June 2026 elections, by reason (late, signature mismatch, missing signature, other), and the number later cured.
What it does
In-person voters must show government ID. The state must issue a free ID card on request. [4]
Every mail-ballot envelope needs the last 4 digits of a government ID chosen at registration. Existing voters must pick one too. [4]
Officials must try to verify citizenship against government data and report county rates each year. The Legislature fills in the details. [4]
Cost: tens of millions to low hundreds of millions a year. [4]
What we're not asking
Design decides everything. Georgia's 2021 ID-number rule produced about 0.6% rejections for ID or signature problems; Texas's 2022 rule produced 12.4%. The difference was clearer forms and envelopes and more accepted ID types (Georgia also takes a state ID number or a photocopy of ID). Prop 39 writes none of that; the Legislature does. [10] [1] [2]
Who writes the rules? A Legislature that opposes the measure. That can mean slow or minimal implementation and litigation, or rules that maximize rejections to make a point.
Citizenship checks. "Best efforts using government data" means database matches, which misfire on naturalized citizens whose records are stale. The measure doesn't say what happens to a voter who can't be verified. [11]
Constitutional and permanent. "Shall only count a ballot after verifying the identity," no guaranteed cure process, and no amendment path except another statewide vote. [11]
Game theory. Out-of-state donors ($17M from Richard Uihlein) are testing a playbook for swing states; both parties fundraise on the fight. [5] [6]
Better or worse? Confidence may rise for some voters. The measurable cost is rejected legitimate ballots in year one and tens to hundreds of millions a year. [4]
Open questions: Would California adopt Georgia's alternatives (state ID number, photocopy)? How many registered voters have no DMV record?
Both sides
For: CA Republican Party, Reform California. Basic ID is normal elsewhere and builds trust.
Against: ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, CA Democratic Party, Sacramento Bee. It solves a non-problem and disenfranchises mail voters.
Poll: 43% of likely voters would vote yes, 55% no. [13]

Some county election officials across Texas say the number of people voting by mail has dropped since 2020, but they’re not sure why.
New research suggests that the recent overhaul of state election laws could explain some of the drop.
A study (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/study-reveals-lasting-voter-suppression-effects-restrictive-texas-law) from the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School looked at Texas voters whose mail ballots or applications to vote by mail were rejected in the 2022 primary, after the state enacted new identification requirements for mail ballots, among other changes. Many of those voters, the study found, appear to have switched to other voting methods or, in some cases, stopped voting.
The study found that 30,000 voters in that primary — or 1 out of 7 voters who started the process to vote by mail — had either their application or ballot rejected, and that “roughly 90% of these individuals did not find another way to participate in the 2022 primary.”
The authors said their findings show the potentially lasting effects of restrictive voting policies on even the most engaged voters.
About 85% of voters whose applications or ballots were rejected had voted in general elections in 2016, 2018, and 2020, said co-author Kevin Morris, a senior research fellow and voting policy scholar with the Brennan Center’s Democracy Program.
“This is a group of people that are super highly engaged in the political process,” Morris told Votebeat. “They have a long history and habit of voting, so to see these effects among them is a big deal.”
The peer-reviewed study, co-authored with political scientists from Barnard College and Tennessee State University, is set to be published later this year in the Journal of Politics (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5264736) and was shared with Votebeat.
After Senate Bill 1, more rejections, less participation
Texas has long had strict limits on voting by mail, allowing it only for certain groups of people, including voters age 65 and up and people with disabilities. Voters who are eligible must apply to use mail ballots each year. If their application is accepted for a primary election, they’ll automatically get a mail ballot for that year’s general election as well. If the application is rejected, they have to reapply.
Become a Votebeat sponsor (https://www.votebeat.org/pages/votebeat-media-kit/)
In 2021, state lawmakers tightened the restrictions as part of an election law overhaul called Senate Bill 1. The legislation required voters to write their driver’s license or personal identification number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number, on the mail ballot application or mail ballot envelope — whichever number they originally used to register. If the ID number was missing or didn’t match the number on file, the application or ballot could be rejected.
The March 2022 primary, the first statewide election after the legislation took effect, saw a dramatic increase in rejection rates: 12,000 absentee ballot applications and more than 24,000 mail ballots were rejected (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), amounting to a 12% rejection rate statewide, far higher than in previous years. In the 2020 presidential election, by comparison, the rejection rate was 1%.
By Texans, for Texans.

Mail-voting applications and ballots of Asian, Latino, and Black Texans were rejected at much higher rates than those of white voters after the ID requirement was added, according to an earlier study (https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2022/10/20/23413651/sb1-mail-ballot-rejections-asian-latino-black-voters/) by the Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/records-show-massive-disenfranchisement-and-racial-disparities-2022-texas).
For the more recent study, researchers obtained individual-level data on mail-voting ballot applications and mail ballots in the 2022 Texas primary from litigation documents and public-records requests to the Texas Secretary of State. They looked at the demographics and the voting history of the roughly 215,000 Texans who requested a mail ballot for that primary, and drilled down to the 30,000 voters who had either their application or ballot rejected.
More than 3,000 voters whose mail-voting applications were rejected voted in person instead in the 2022 primary.
Out of the more than 18,000 voters whose mail ballots were rejected, only 344 voted in person. The others did not ultimately vote in the primary.
The study said the rejections increased what it called the “cost of voting,” because voters had to “try to sort out why their mail ballot did not arrive, re-apply for an absentee ballot, and seek out details about where to vote in-person.”
“I can’t speak to any law other than SB 1,” Morris said, “but this does provide some evidence that the effect of being disenfranchised does make people even less likely to vote into the future.”
County officials observe the impact of new restrictions
Before the passage of SB 1, mail voters were not required to provide identification numbers, and although they still had to apply each year, election officials were allowed to send them reminders to resubmit their applications. The new law made such unsolicited reminders illegal.
In some counties, election officials said they’ve personally observed how the law’s requirements have affected voter participation and the way people vote.
Become a Votebeat sponsor (https://www.votebeat.org/pages/votebeat-media-kit/)
Lisa Hayes, the elections administrator in Guadalupe County east of San Antonio, said that participation in mail voting rose in 2020, when the state allowed voters to hand-deliver their mail-in ballot during the early voting period because of the pandemic. During that year’s presidential election, Guadalupe County sent out more than 8,000 mail-in ballots to qualifying voters, and 90% were returned.
Since the new requirements passed in 2021, fewer people are voting by mail, Hayes said, and she’s seen voters become more frustrated.
For the November 2022 general election, the county sent out 3,354 mail-in ballots to voters. The return rate for that election was 81%. The return rate for the November 2024 presidential election went up slightly up to 84%, she said.
SB 1 included a provision that allows voters to correct errors on their application. Hayes said that in the period leading up to an election, her office is constantly answering calls from frustrated voters whose applications need to be corrected and resubmitted.
If the voter’s mail-voting application is missing one of the two required ID numbers, a signature, or the explanation of why they qualify to vote by mail, the elections office mails the voter a notice and a new application so they can correct it. Hayes said if voters correct one issue but fail to fix another, they must start the process over.
“Unfortunately, the voters have to jump through so many hoops to get into that corrective-action loop, that they just get frustrated and they give up,” Hayes said. In some cases, voters will send in two or three corrected applications before they get approved. Others opt to vote in person instead.
“These are the voters we’re supposed to be trying to help,” she said. “They need the help. They need to vote by mail. It’s not just a convenience for them, it’s a need. So of course they’re frustrated.”
Diana Leggett, 83, volunteers helping people who live at assisted-living facilities and nursing homes in Cooke and Grayson counties in North Texas. In 2022, she focused on helping seniors to navigate the new mail ballot rules.
“When you’re 90 years old, you’ve voted all your life, but you sure as heck don’t remember what you put down the first time you registered to vote,” Leggett said, referring to the requirement that ID numbers match what’s on file. “Some don’t have a driver’s license anymore or don’t know the number.”
When residents had their mail ballot applications rejected, she said, they often didn’t try again.
Become a Votebeat sponsor (https://www.votebeat.org/pages/votebeat-media-kit/)
To keep voters from becoming frustrated, election officials have had to find ways to ensure voters are aware of the requirements to vote by mail.
Kaleb Breaux, election administrator for Collin County in North Texas, said his staff recalls the 2022 primary as a “rough mail ballot election.”
The county had over 7,000 mail-in ballots, and over 700 were rejected due to the new ID requirements, he said. To help voters, he said, his office began to insert instructions with the applications and the ballots “to help draw voters’ attention” to the sections with the new requirements. And it helped.
In the November general election, Breaux said, the county rejected just 85 ballots for ID requirement issues.

### Proposal
***Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote.*** Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California.

Did the Trump administration just prove that voter fraud in California is a nonfactor?
By Raheem Hosseini (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/raheem-hosseini/) , Staff Writer Updated Oct 20, 2026 2:45 p.m.
Peter Hosey carries a ballot after a No Kings protest in San Francisco on Saturday. The demonstration emphasized early voting in California for the 2026 midterm elections.
Benjamin Fanjoy/For the S.F. Chronicle
In its siege on California’s election authority (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/election-mail-ballot-california-22465892.php), the Trump administration has grown louder about its certainty of widespread voter fraud even as its evidence has dwindled sharply.
Back in July, the Department of Homeland Security announced (https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/17/dhs-secretary-markwayne-mullin-sends-letters-secretaries-state-warning-about-non) that a preliminary investigation turned up more than 190,000 potential noncitizens who they believed were illegally registered in the state.
By October, the figure was down to roughly 20,000 as the Department of Justice sent demands (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/doj-california-ballots-22476975.php) to California and Los Angeles elections officials and then sued them (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/doj-california-ballots-lawsuit-22478986.php) in a case that election law experts say is shockingly thin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/doj-california-ballot-lawsuit-election-22479436.php).

On Monday, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Los Angeles announced (https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/11-foreign-nationals-arrested-california-federal-charges-alleging-they-illegally) as part of an election-fraud investigation called “Operation Protect the Vote” the arrests of 28 Californians, all of them legal residents, that “prove what we have been saying,” in the words of First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli.
Of the 28 charged, 23 people have been accused of voting illegally, allegedly casting 34 illegal ballots in elections dating back to 2020, including one provisional ballot.
If it can prove its allegations, the Trump administration will have revised its initial estimate of voter fraud in California down by a factor of 8,300 — a fact federal officials tried to spin in their favor in their charging announcement.
“Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week,” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said Monday in a statement. “California refused to look at that list. Today’s charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk.”

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter listens during a Sept. 22 news conference on election integrity in Washington, D.C.
Kent Nishimura/AFP/TNS According to the California Secretary of State’s Office (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results), almost 94 million ballots have been cast in the eight statewide elections since November 2020. The 34 allegedly illegal ballots would account for 0.00004% of them.
“The arrest of 28 people for potentially registering or voting while noncitizens is tiny compared to the 23 million California voters,” UCLA Law School professor Rick Hasen, director of his school’s Safeguarding Democracy Project (https://law.ucla.edu/academics/centers/safeguarding-democracy-project?_gl=1*1ddn0c8*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTE0Nzg1NTIxOC4xNzkyNDUwNTA1*_ga_LH03WX2T8B*czE3OTI0NTA1MDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTI0NTA1MDQkajYwJGwwJGgw), wrote on his blog (https://electionlawblog.org/2026/us-government-pre-dawn-raid-to-arrest-purported-non-citizen-registering-to-vote-is-meant-to-obscure-the-small-number-of-noncitizen-voters-that-doj-his-found-in-california/) Monday. “By DOJ’s own account, some of these people only registered to vote, and did not vote. So we are talking about a drop in the bucket. If DOJ could prove many more cases, we would have heard about it.”
The same pattern unfolded against other blue states the Trump administration accused of rampant fraud.
In Pennsylvania, where DHS claimed (https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/17/dhs-secretary-markwayne-mullin-sends-letters-secretaries-state-warning-about-non) it had identified more than 14,000 potential noncitizen voters, only four people were charged (https://www.justice.gov/usao-edpa/pr/four-non-citizens-charged-illegally-voting-2024-election) with illegally voting in 2024. In Nevada, where DHS claimed nearly 16,000 (https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/17/dhs-secretary-markwayne-mullin-sends-letters-secretaries-state-warning-about-non) noncitizens were illegally registered, that figure was reduced to 185 (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/24/dhs-nevada-voter-non-citizens-error) and then to zero (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/us/politics/nevada-voters-homeland-security-trump.html) as everyone on the list proved to be a citizen.

McCotter defended the federal government’s record in a news conference (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zmZq3DrhwOM) Monday, even as he acknowledged the likelihood of more error.
“There may be some names on there who it turns out ultimately are citizens. We’re not perfect and that’s why we’ve asked California to cooperate with us,” McCotter told reporters. “These are the ones where we’re kind of the most confident that they are noncitizens.”
Gov. Gavin Newsom pounced on the admission on X (https://x.com/GovPressOffice/status/2112242722052665820) and also mocked (https://x.com/GovPressOffice/status/2112247407366885766) Essayli for acknowledging that some of the people the federal government charged hadn’t actually voted. “YIKES. Stephen Miller not going to be happy about this performance,” Newsom posted, referring to the senior White House adviser.
Essayli also acknowledged that the federal government has yet to show California evidence of its claims, and instead wants full access to the state’s voter rolls.
The Trump administration has lost 26 federal court cases to do just that, with judges calling the request illegal and an invasion of voters’ privacy.

“We want to run their voter rolls through our federal immigration databases. California is refusing to do that,” Essayli told reporters. “They want to look inside our systems. … We’re happy to show a lot of our work, most of our work, but California has to come to the table and be willing to open their books as well.”
In a court filing (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28825536-usvscal/) Tuesday, Los Angeles County election officials said they tried to check the federal government’s claims and found them lacking substance.
Along with noting that federal law prohibited election officials from making substantive changes to voter registration lists within 90 days of an election, Assistant Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Aman Bhullar said only 7,035 of the more than 20,000 voters the federal government flagged had addresses in Los Angeles County. Bhullar, head of his department’s technology bureau, also said that a preliminary analysis of 200 of the flagged voter records determined that 112 had already been canceled or considered inactive and hadn’t received ballots, and that more than 70% had no record of voting.
The government’s process for assembling its lists of suspected noncitizen registrants came up in a federal court hearing Monday in Oakland. State and national nurses unions, voting rights groups and the counties of San Francisco and Santa Clara are challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s secretive process for flagging voters and subjecting them to investigation that plaintiffs said likely amounted to illegal voter intimidation.
“The government is sweeping with an extremely broad net,” Geoffrey Curfman, an attorney with Protect Democracy, said in court. Noting how the Trump administration’s estimates keep coming down, he contended that there’s a “substantial risk that U.S. citizens will be swept up and targeted in these investigations.”

Article continues below this ad
Assistant U.S. Attorney Kelsey Helland countered that plaintiffs had failed to find an example of a U.S. citizen being interrogated for voter fraud.
“How many citizens are being interviewed when they should not be?” Helland challenged. “That is a question mark. They have the evidentiary burden here.”
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín said she was leaning toward siding with plaintiffs that the federal government had violated aspects of the Voting Rights Act.
Election law experts say the Trump administration has an unprecedented credibility issue.
“If I believed the Department of Justice that there was evidence to suggest that there actually are 20,000-plus ineligible people potentially casting ballots in California, then I might feel differently. But I don’t believe that and I don’t believe that they’ve provided any evidence to suggest that it is true,” said Sean Morales-Doyle, the senior director of the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program. “And based on all of the similarly ridiculous claims which have proven to be false coming out of this administration thus far, I’m very skeptical.”
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research in Washington D.C., said the federal government has also been disingenuous about its claims of wanting to simply tidy up the voter rolls.
The former Justice Department attorney said a DOJ acting in good faith would have contacted states at the beginning of an odd-numbered year, well before elections were underway, and shared their intelligence. Instead, he said, the Trump administration singled out four blue states, made unsubstantiated claims about 250,000 noncitizen voters in July, and then “went silent” until ballots were mailed out to California’s 23 million registered voters.
“I don’t know what their motivation is, but I can tell you what their motivation isn’t,” Becker told reporters in a virtual briefing Thursday. “Because if they were seeking to work in good faith to clean up the voter lists that they believe had issues, they would’ve done this months ago in a much different fashion. However, it does raise questions as to whether or not the sole purpose of this is to set the stage for false claims about election theft after an election that the president might be worried his party was going to do poorly in.”
The Constitution gives the authority for running elections — and managing lists of voters — to the states. California and its counties update their voter registration lists multiple times a day, say the officials responsible for overseeing them and those familiar with the process.
“It is something that is happening every single minute of every day,” said Tricia Webber, Santa Cruz County Clerk and president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials.
The process is both automated and manual, vertical and horizontal, and pulls from various federal, state and local data sources: VoteCal, the state’s centralized voter registration database; the DMV, state Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, U.S. Postal Service, courts, public health agencies and more. If everything matches perfectly and comes up clean, a new or updated registration is processed automatically. If there is a slight discrepancy — like a Charles reregisters as Charlie — it’s flagged for a manual check, Weber said.
“It’s just a continual process, and we’re getting information from a lot of different sources,” she said.
Even before the Trump administration turned its latest actions against California into a promotional music video (https://x.com/TheJusticeDept/status/2112563468108714151), Becker sounded nostalgic for the days of Bush-Gore.
He worked in the U.S. Department of Justice in 2000, when Vice President Al Gore and Texas Gov. George W. Bush were locked in a highly contested dispute over a too-close-to-call race for the nation’s highest office. Considering he was at a DOJ that belonged to President Bill Clinton’s administration, he wasn’t surprised when his marching orders came down.
“I remember very clearly, as a voting section attorney, getting guidance and instructions that we were to do absolutely nothing with regard to the 2000 presidential election,” Becker recalled Thursday. “That both sides were very well represented by counsel, that it was going to be argued in court with the candidates and the parties arguing it out, and that we would take a step back as the DOJ and not interfere in any way. That was not despite of, but because of the fact that the vice president of the United States was a candidate for president.”
The Supreme Court eventually decided the race for Bush. Clinton and Gore left office in January 2001, and the republic soldiered on through 12 more national elections. Even after President Barack Obama peacefully transferred power to President Donald Trump in 2016, Becker said the DOJ remained adherent to its long-standing practice of not conducting election investigations in close proximity to elections.
But then, last week, two weeks before the midterms, the DOJ sued to stop California from counting more than 20,000 ballots from potential voters the federal government claims, without evidence, were mailed to noncitizens.
“It should trouble most of us,” Becker said, “particularly given the fact in the California case they appear to have intentionally gamed the system, to wait until the last minute to cause the most chaos.”
